entries.title: Abhishek Sharma hits ton as India beat New Zealand by 6 wickets in 3rd T20
entries.summary: The opening pair put on 133-run partnership as India chased down 199 to wrap up the five-match T20 series.
entries.content:
The opening pair put on 133-run partnership as India chased down 199 to wrap up the five-match T20I series.

An aggressive partnership between Abhishek Sharma and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi propelled India to a six-wicket win and a series victory over New Zealand in Wellington.

India sewed up the five-match Twenty20 International (T20I) series on Tuesday with two games to spare, chasing down New Zealand’s total of 198 in just 13.2 overs, with Abhishek blasting 113 and Sooryavanshi 45.

The opening pair’s 133-run partnership in just 7.1 overs obliterated the New Zealand bowling attack with one of the most destructive partnerships in T20I history.

Jacob Duffy’s first over went for 26 runs, and the openers never let up.

Abhishek hit nine fours and 11 sixes in his 38-ball knock, receiving a standing ovation when he eventually fell to the bowling of Kyle Jamieson.

By that stage, India had reached 178-2 in just 10 overs.

“The key was pretty simple: Vaibhav and I enjoyed our time,” Abhishek said of their partnership.

“When we were fielding, we saw there was some extra bounce. Vaibhav started off well, and we took the momentum from there.”

Sooryavanshi was promoted to open alongside Abhishek after batting at number three in the second T20I, hitting four fours and four sixes in his 19-ball innings.

“Getting 100 in five overs – I have not seen that before at the international level,” India captain Shreyas Iyer said.

“Credit where it is due, the way they played was exceptional.”

India won the toss for the third time in three matches and again elected to bowl.

Bhuvneshwar Kumar and Arshdeep Singh extracted prodigious seam from the pitch, beating the outside edge of New Zealand openers Tim Seifert and Finn Allen.

Seifert was removed top-edging Singh for two, before Daryl Mitchell joined Allen and combined for an 86-run partnership.

Mitchell was quick to assess the conditions and moved around the crease to counteract the seam movement.

He seized on any short deliveries with powerful strikes to the short square boundaries, hitting five fours and five sixes on his way to 89 from 52 balls.

Allen made 40 from 25 balls before departing, and Mitchell found another powerful partner in Bevon Jacobs, who hit an unbeaten 39 from 23 deliveries.

The fourth T20I is at Auckland’s Eden Park on Friday.

entries.title: Media groups challenge India’s privacy law at top court
entries.summary: News organisations are challenging the law, arguing it could hamper investigative journalism and endanger sources.
entries.content:
News organisations are challenging the law, arguing it could hamper investigative journalism and endanger sources.

The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounts to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups have told the Supreme Court.

A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s law on Tuesday, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow the government to identify journalists’ sources, according to The Indian Express newspaper.

“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), told judges.

“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission … it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”

The Supreme Court said it would hear the case next month.

Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written exemption for journalists as in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.

The DNPA’s members include Ambani’s Network18, which has seven digital news platforms, Adani’s NDTV and other high-profile media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.

Fear of putting sources at risk

A key concern in the law is the requirement of consent, says the group’s filing, cited by the Reuters news agency.

A social media platform or online retailer can seek consent from users when they sign up, but the DNPA has argued that requiring a journalist to notify the subject of an investigation and seek consent “would allow that subject to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses”.

The law also lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand that their data be erased, without any public-interest safeguard, which the DNPA says could force its members to unpublish or heavily redact a factual news report.

News publishers are concerned that a federal authority created under the law can impose fines for noncompliance, and grants powers to New Delhi to block access to any information in the “interests of the general public”, which would curtail press freedom, the DNPA said.

From next year, the law will also let New Delhi order any organisation handling personal data “to furnish such information as it may call for”, putting newsrooms at risk of having to divulge sources, the filing said.

It can also deter whistleblowers from sharing information on corruption, corporate wrongdoing or electoral malpractice with reporters, the DNPA argued.

The “nakedly unguided” provision must be quashed, the DNPA said, adding that the power “can extend to privileged communications in possession of a reporter or the informant.”

Families of victims killed in Jordanian strike deny links to church attack

entries.title: Why Jordan has struck Syria: What we know
entries.summary: Syria says Jordan did not coordinate with Damascus before launching operation in rural Deraa and Suwayda.
entries.content:
Syria says Jordan did not coordinate with Damascus before launching operation in rural Deraa and Suwayda.

Jordan said its air force conducted retaliatory attacks on what it called “dens of terrorist organizations in southern Syria”, linked to suspects accused of being behind last week’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the kingdom.

In a post on X, the Jordanian Armed Forces said: “Fighter jets from the Royal Air Force destroyed a number of terrorist sites in southeastern Syria.

“The operation resulted in the killing and wounding of many elements of the terrorist organizations and the destruction of a number of their vehicles,” Jordan’s Armed Forces added.

“The armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with ⁠Damascus.” Jordan’s military said in a further post on X.

ISIL (ISIS) has claimed responsibility for the October 23 church attack.

Jordan did not specify the locations of the attacks or provide casualty figures.

What is Syria saying?

Syria has contradicted Jordan’s account of the overnight attacks.

In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed Jordan of its “complete reservation” over the attacks, which took place “without prior coordination or notification with the Syrian side”.

A Foreign Ministry official told Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett that the strikes were a “treacherous attack”.

Pett reported from Syria that authorities have said seven people were killed, including three children, in Jordanian air attacks on Deraa and Suwayda countryside.

Syria’s Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management said its teams had responded to attacks in four sites.

Syria’s civil defence agency said it had recovered the bodies of those killed in attacks. They include five members of one family, including three children and a woman who were killed together in a strike on a tent in the village of al-Taff, in the Lajat area of northeastern Deraa province. Three other members of the family were injured, it said.

In the al-Shayah farms near Nassib, in Deraa countryside, a strike on a farm killed Riyad Karrad, 80. His body was taken to Deraa National Hospital.

In Muzayrib, in the Ein al-Basal area of western Deraa countryside, a strike hit a home. No casualties were reported.

In the town of Shuhayb, in northern Suwayda countryside, a strike on a home killed Mutlaq Abu al-Khail, 60. Rescue teams were still working to recover his body from the rubble when the report was issued.

There was no immediate comment from Jordan on Syria’s accusations that civilians – not armed fighters – were killed.

Shortly after the attacks, Syrian customs authorities on Tuesday closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan, the only passenger and commercial traffic pathway between the neighbours.

Why did Jordan attack Syrian sites?

Jordan said its attacks on Syrian territory were in response to an attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.

On Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout over the violence that killed nine people in a rare attack on the minority Christian community in Jordan on Friday.

Major-General Obaidullah al-Maaytah, Jordan’s director of public security, named the three detained suspects as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.

The attack during a funeral prompted Jordan’s King Abdullah II to order security forces to respond with an “iron fist”.

Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazin al-Farrayeh said he was launching an investigation “examining all the circumstances that lead young people towards extremism”.

“The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are ⁠no indications of any links between them and other cells,” al-Farrayeh added.

Has Jordan struck Syrian territory in the past?

Jordan has conducted multiple air attacks on Syria since 2023, saying it was targeting drug and arms smugglers.

The operations have sometimes hit civilians.

Human Rights Watch demanded accountability after Jordan launched attacks that killed women and children in January 2024.

“Cross-border airstrikes that kill civilians demand scrutiny regardless of the threat posed by drug smuggling from southern Syria,” Human Rights Watch said.

The Jordanian Armed Forces said its operations along its border were aimed at armed groups reportedly carrying narcotics, arms, and explosives that it suspected are linked to Iran-allied groups.

How will Syria respond to Jordan’s latest attack?

Syria’s Foreign Ministry said it was in contact with Jordan to establish the circumstances of the operation.

Damascus said it will address the aftermath of the attacks while “safeguarding Syria’s security and sovereignty”.

entries.title: ‘It’s magical’: London’s iconic Oxford Street goes vehicle-free
entries.summary: The cars have gone, and so have the buses, but while retailers expect a boost, residents worry about change.
entries.content:
The cars have gone, and so have the buses, but while retailers expect a boost, residents worry about change.

London, United Kingdom – “It’s magical,” says biology teacher Muneera Alfadhel from under her umbrella.

In fact, it is a characteristically rainy, grey day in London, but the weather is doing nothing to dampen her mood. She is among the first to walk down the middle of the iconic Oxford Street following its pedestrianisation.

For generations, shoppers have bustled along Oxford Street next to bikes, cars, black cabs and red double-decker buses. But on Monday, from Great Portland Street to Orchard Street, the road is now a pedestrian-only zone.

On Monday morning, by force of habit, most pedestrians are still sticking to the pavement. Mark Arbouine, a forensic scientist out for a stroll, is one of the few breaking ranks: “I saw there was no traffic today, so I thought, why not walk in the middle of the street and take advantage of it? I just think it’s great for the environment, great for shopping. It’s just so much easier to move around the street.”

This tiny strip of real estate is big business: about 1 percent of the UK’s annual gross domestic product (GDP) is generated along this 1km (0.6 miles) stretch of street. But despite its outsized importance, Oxford Street has in recent decades been hit by lower consumer spending, as well as falling rents and footfall, which is now just 57 percent of what it was in 2006, according to New West End Company, a retail trade body.

The Greater London Authority, also known as City Hall, believes pedestrianisation could, therefore, offer a lifeline.

City Hall analysis suggests the partial pedestrianisation of Oxford Street could generate more than $109m per year and support an additional 700 jobs. Following a weekend trial in October 2025, two-thirds of businesses in the area said they had higher or similar sales figures during the pedestrianisation.

This is the first step in a multi-phase regeneration project to add two public squares, 50 trees and hundreds of public seating.

Barbara Stoll, a leading campaigner on the benefits of greener, more walkable cities, was smiling as she observed the street. The air already feels cleaner, she noted.

“It’s amazing coming here this morning. Walking down the street, it was already so uplifting that the noise is considerably lower,” she said. “People are excited. I saw people coming up from the tube and looking around. Seeing that, it’s almost like children when it’s Christmas Day.

“So I think it’s absolutely wonderful, and so needed for London.”

Residents ‘haven’t really been listened to’

On Saturday, ahead of the change, not all shoppers were convinced. A French tourist said he would avoid Oxford Street altogether if buses and cabs were no longer allowed through.

“People with disabilities who cannot walk a lot – that would be really helpful if the buses move on and they don’t discontinue [them],” a shopper told Al Jazeera.

“It would be good. Sometimes you’re tired; sometimes it’s raining.”

The pedestrianisation of Oxford Street has been years in the making, and not without controversy.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan first tried it in 2017, following a manifesto pledge. But the plan fell apart in 2018, when Westminster Council – the local government authority responsible for Oxford Street at the time – withdrew its backing, saying residents did not support it.

Following a public consultation, Khan created the Oxford Street Development Corporation, taking responsibility for the street away from local officials and transferring it to the Greater London Authority and Transport for London.

With this second, successful attempt at pedestrianisation, doubts from local authorities have not gone away.

Residents are not being listened to, said Councillor Tim Barnes, the deputy leader and cabinet member for growth and planning for the City of Westminster.

“There has been a communication process with residents, but it’s been pretty much one way. Mostly, they are being told what’s going to happen to them and how it’s going to happen; what the format of the process is going to be in future. But realistically, those who know the street best haven’t really been listened to.”

He believes the economic benefits are overstated and do not consider the impact of displacing bus routes from a major road to the surrounding, smaller streets. That fear is shared by resident Nerma Cridge, who said London’s West End will become “completely unliveable, too crowded and too noisy at night”.

“We think all of this should be done in a much more productive relationship with communities,” she told Al Jazeera over the phone.

‘People just take back the space’

Concerns over the change will fade once residents see the real-world results in the coming months, Stoll believes.

“Examples from across Europe and the world, where such projects have already happened, prove that this only makes life better overall for local residents,” she said.

“Retail gets a boost. More people linger, more people come to the street, more people spend money in the shops, and even local shop vacancies reduce. The local air pollution significantly reduces, and as activity increases, people just take back the space.”

The Oxford Street Development Corporation will be testing and reviewing the results of the pedestrianisation in the coming months, and reviewing its findings early next year. Transitioning the rest of Oxford Street into a permanent, traffic-free public space is expected to go ahead by the end of next year.

Ahead of mayoral elections in 2028, the pedestrianisation could be one of the last major initiatives that Sadiq Khan signs off. A landmark project that will also become his legacy.

entries.title: WNBA Finals: Valkyries beat Dream to reach the brink of their first title
entries.summary: Kiah Stokes and Veronica Burton shine for Golden State as Angel Reese's Atlanta team was stifled by a strong defence.
entries.content:
Kiah Stokes and Veronica Burton shine for Golden State as Angel Reese’s Atlanta team was stifled by a strong defence.

Kiah Stokes and Veronica Burton each scored 13 points to help secure Golden State’s 64-55 victory over Atlanta, putting the Valkyries on the brink of winning the Women’s NBA Finals.

Tiffany Hayes and reserve Cecilia Zandalasini each added 12 points for the Valkyries while Stokes and Burton each pulled down a team-best eight rebounds in Game 5 on Monday.

Golden State seized a 3-2 lead over the Dream in the best-of-seven championship series, which continues on Thursday in Atlanta.

“We’re not done yet. We’ve got one more,” Stokes said. “We need two hoops, 94 feet and each other and that’s all we need.”

The Valkyries, in only their second WNBA campaign, kept Dream star Angel Reese to seven points on 2-of-8 shooting, although she grabbed a game-high 15 rebounds.

Golden State dominated defensively, keeping Atlanta to a season-low in points on 19-of-65 (29 percent) shooting from the floor.

“That has just been our staple all season. We really rely on our defence,” Stokes said.

“They are tough. We have to make sure we’re all doing our part. It’s a team for a reason.”

Stokes had a game-high four blocked shots and has had at least three blocks in every finals game.

Rhyne Howard led Atlanta with 20 points while Jordin Canada added 12.

The Valkyries have been a hit with spectators in the home arena of the NBA Golden State Warriors.

“You all are amazing,” Stokes screamed to a cheering crowd moments after the triumph. “We couldn’t do this without you all.”
